fundamental.thesis: Allied Blenders and Distillers is one of India's largest IMFL companies, maker of the mass-to-premium Officer's Choice whisky brand, competing in a highly regulated alcobev market where state excise pass-throughs dominate gross revenues (implied ~₹7,500+ cr) while net revenue (post-levies) is a fraction at ₹757 cr for FY26. FY26 consolidated net revenue declined 6.2% YoY — a multi-quarter deterioration from +3.9% growth in 9M FY25 to −7.8% in 9M FY26, with only a marginal recovery to −6.2% by year-end — though EBITDA surged 25.8% to ₹568 cr (margin expanded to 7.5% from 4.9%) and PAT rose 17.2% to ₹228 cr, making this a cost-compression-driven result against persistent volume headwinds rather than any volume-recovery story; volume growth, the FMCG sector card's primary signal for sustainable demand, is absent. Trailing P/E of 77.26× is materially above the FMCG/alcobev sector benchmark of 40–65× and ranks at P87 vs broad-market peers — firmly expensive — and while forward P/E of 39.87× falls within the lower end of the sector range, it is premised on a unanimous all-buy sell-side consensus whose EPS estimates are already tracking −5.6% lower over 90 days, a classic pre-derating pattern. The margin-expansion thesis is fragile against declining revenues, very high financial leverage (D/E 68.25; finance costs ₹134.65 cr consume ~59% of PAT), an unresolved income-tax investigation (initial demand ₹3,512 cr, appealed but still live at ₹26 cr recognised for FY26), and an ongoing CSD trade-rate arbitration (₹33.98 cr) — any one of these could inflect the earnings trajectory sharply downward.

fundamental.thesis: Asahi India Glass (AIS) is India's dominant integrated glass manufacturer serving automotive OEM/replacement and architectural segments, with recent capacity additions in float glass (Soniyana), automotive (Patan), and windows (south plant) underpinning the medium-term growth story. Revenue growth has been modest and choppy — FY25 +5.5%, Q1FY26 +9.1%, then collapsing to -0.1% in Q2FY26 before recovering to +6.5% on a 9M FY26 basis — while PAT has deteriorated sharply: 9M FY26 PAT declined 23.9% YoY (₹212 cr vs ₹279 cr) with PAT margins compressing from 8.1% in FY25 to 5.8% in 9M FY26, driven by higher depreciation and interest charges from the recent capex cycle. At a trailing P/E of 62.23×, the stock sits at P79 among 471 broad-market peers, a 76% premium to the market median (35.4×), and trades far above the auto-ancillary sector benchmark of 18–28× P/E; using EV/EBITDA (the preferred yardstick for this capital-intensive business) at 26.73× it ranks at P59, and P/B of 5.58× against a weak ROE of 10.5% confirms an expensive valuation on any lens — grade: expensive. The primary risk is that the Board-approved ₹2,000 crore greenfield capex (float, coatings, processing) will further elevate D/E (already high at ~56%) and extend the depreciation/interest drag, prolonging margin compression at a time when sell-side EPS estimates are already being cut (-7.4% in 30 days), making a valuation de-rating the path of least resistance.

ICICI Bank is India's second-largest private sector lender by assets (₹23.7L cr standalone; ₹29.1L cr consolidated), with a diversified retail-focused loan book and a management team with a demonstrated track record of disciplined, risk-calibrated growth. Q4FY26 consolidated PAT grew 9.3% YoY; revenue growth has decelerated from +9.2% to +7.6% across recent filing windows, yet asset quality improved materially — GNPA fell to 1.40% (from 1.58% in H1-FY26) and net NPA reached a best-in-class 0.33%, with credit cost benign at just 38 bps and PCR strong at 75.8%. Using P/B + ROE — the correct yardstick for lenders per the sector card — P/B of 2.48× against ROE of 16.4% grades as FAIR: not cheap (peer-relative P/B ranks P93, a 69% premium to the sector median driven by quality justifiably), not expensive (P/B > 3× with ROE < 12% would be the expensive threshold; ICICI clears both tests), and trailing P/E of 16.82× sits at the upper end of the 12–18× sector range while forward P/E of 13.82× signals ~18–20% expected EPS growth ahead. The single biggest structural risk is that deposit growth (11.4% YoY) continues to lag loan growth (15.8% YoY), tightening the funding gap and forcing reliance on costlier wholesale borrowings; management has already guided NIMs 'range-bound' in FY27, capping the benefit from the ongoing RBI easing cycle and constraining NII upside.

On accessible non-P/E metrics, P/B of 3.94× against a negative ROE of -8.9% grades expensive (P/B premium with value destruction is a red flag); EV/EBITDA is negative (meaningless); the primary developer yardstick of EV/pre-sales cannot be computed due to missing booking data, so the valuation grade is tentative. The sell-side is unanimously bullish (11/0/0 buy) with a 46.8% target upside, but next-year EPS estimates have been cut 27–29% over 90 days — a pre-derating pattern — while a D/E ratio of 152.37 in a loss-making phase leaves no balance-sheet buffer if the cycle softens.

fundamental.thesis: Navin Fluorine International is a specialty fluorochemicals franchise producing refrigerant gases, high-performance products, and CRAMS, occupying a high-barrier fluorochemistry niche that benefits structurally from China+1 supply-chain realignment in pharma and specialty chemicals. Q3FY26 consolidated revenue accelerated to +47.2% YoY (₹892 cr) with PAT surging 121.6% YoY to ₹185 cr — continuing a sharp multi-quarter recovery from FY25's -10% revenue and 9.0% PAT margin — with EBITDA margins expanding to 33.1% and PAT margins to 20.8%, driven by destocking unwinding and operating leverage at near-peak capacity utilisation (95% in H1FY26). Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card for this capital-intensive specialty business, the stock trades at 34.61× — well above the 5-8× mid-cycle benchmark for specialty chemicals and even above quality-premium ranges of 15-20× — placing it at P73 vs broad-market peers with the sell-side consensus target -2.4% below the current price, warranting an 'expensive' grade despite strong fundamentals. Capacity utilisation at 95% limits near-term volume upside until new capacity is commissioned, finance costs surged 79% YoY to ₹88.91 cr in 9M FY26 signalling elevated leverage, and the stock at 92.7% of its 52-week range prices in near-perfection, leaving little margin of safety if demand or execution disappoints.

fundamental.thesis: Granules India is a mid-cap integrated pharma manufacturer (API → PFI → finished dosage) focused on high-volume molecules — paracetamol, ibuprofen, metformin, guaifenesin — with approximately 60–70% export revenue skewed toward US generics, making FDA compliance a core earnings variable. FY26 consolidated revenue grew +19.7% YoY to ₹5,366cr with PAT up +18.6% to ₹595cr (11.1% margin), a meaningful recovery from FY25's flat -0.6% revenue decline; Q3FY26 quarterly momentum further accelerated to +22.0% YoY revenue and +27.7% PAT growth, confirming a genuine recovery arc from the FDA-disrupted FY25 base — however, PAT margin for FY26 at 11.1% was essentially flat vs FY25's 11.2%, with rising finance costs (+10.8% YoY from acquisition debt) capping margin expansion despite volume recovery. Using the pharma sector yardstick (trailing P/E 28–40x sector median), Granules at 31.96x sits in the mid-band — rated fair; EV/EBITDA of 15.94x (P30 vs broad market, -29.5% discount to peer median) and forward P/E collapsing to 20.08x signal the market already prices in a strong earnings recovery, but with the stock at 94% of its 52-week range and sell-side consensus target essentially at spot price, the risk/reward is asymmetric to the downside if the FDA overhang re-emerges. The outstanding USFDA warning letter for Gagillapur (voluntary manufacturing pause Sep 2024, three-consultant remediation ongoing with no clearance yet) is an unresolved binary risk that could escalate to import alert and directly impair the US revenue base.

fundamental.thesis: EIH Limited (The Oberoi Group) is India's pre-eminent luxury hotel chain, operating premium Oberoi and mid-scale Trident properties with a structurally advantaged RevPAR position in a market where hotel supply still lags demand through ~2027; using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick (appropriate for capital-intensive hotel assets), the stock trades at 18.0×, a 20% discount to the broad-market peer median of 22.6×, and a forward P/E of 21.6× well below the trailing 31.5×, implying the market is already pricing in a meaningful FY27 earnings recovery — making the valuation verdict 'fair'. FY26 revenues grew +7.2% YoY to ₹2,940 cr (decelerating from +10% in FY25 and a temporary H1FY26 low of +5%), while PAT contracted sharply -15% to ₹628 cr as margins compressed from 26.7% to 21.4% — largely attributable to ₹131–132 cr in exceptional charges (Kolkata property renovation de-recognition, Mashobra write-downs, ₹29 cr Labour Code liability), and Q3FY26 EBITDA margin of 48.9% in the peak season confirms the underlying hotel operations remain high-quality when stripped of one-offs. The biggest risk is that Labour Code wage inflation proves structurally elevated (not a one-time item) and converges with any moderation in RevPAR growth as new luxury supply enters, permanently resetting the margin band below FY25's 26.7% PAT level.

fundamental.thesis: Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals is a leading consumer durables company in fans, pumps, lighting, and small appliances (via the Butterfly brand), competing in India's mass-to-mid urban segment where category growth has stalled against a premiumisation tide that favours aspirational brands. Full-year FY26 revenue grew only +2.9% YoY to ₹8,096 cr — decelerating sharply from 9M FY25's +8.4% — with the core ECS segment (75% of revenue) expanding just 1.43%, while PAT swung to a net loss of ₹-242 cr on a ₹716 cr non-cash impairment of the Butterfly acquisition; the underlying Q3FY26 quarter was healthier (+7.3% revenue growth, 5.2% PAT margin), but the full-year PAT margin trajectory has contracted from +6.7% to -3.0%. Trailing P/E is unavailable due to the loss year; forward P/E of 23.94× and EV/EBITDA of 20.0× sit near the broad-market peer median (P44 on EV/EBITDA), pointing to fair valuation, but P/B of 6.02× against a negative ROE of -6.3% raises value-trap risk, and 90-day sell-side estimate cuts of -6.2% for next-FY while 91% of analysts maintain a buy rating is the textbook pre-derating pattern. The biggest risk is that the Butterfly impairment marks permanent capital destruction, and as estimate cuts compound, the 'fair' forward multiple is likely understating the true re-rating risk.

3M India is the listed subsidiary of 3M Company (USA), a diversified industrial conglomerate operating across Safety & Industrial, Transportation & Electronics, Healthcare, and Consumer segments in India — a high-quality, asset-light franchise with strong pricing power and brand moat. FY26 full-year revenue grew a steady +14.5% to ₹5,090 cr with all segments in double digits, but PAT growth of +9.7% (₹522 cr) materially lagged revenue, dragged by a one-off APA tax settlement of ₹139.47 cr and a Labour Code exceptional charge of ₹34.33 cr; stripping those out, underlying operating momentum is solid — EBITDA grew 23.2% with margins expanding to 20.3% from 18.9% — though Q3FY26 PAT went deeply negative (-₹62 cr) due to the APA hit, distorting the PAT margin trajectory. Valuation is unambiguously expensive: trailing P/E of 71.5× is roughly double the Industrials sector median (28–45×), EV/EBITDA of 36.4× sits at the P76 percentile vs broad peers, and P/B of 21.3× places it at the P97 percentile — the high ROE of 28.9% partially justifies the premium P/B but not the full extent of the P/E premium, and forward P/E of 44.1× still sits ~100% above the broad-market median, leaving limited margin of safety. The single biggest risk is a de-rating event: at 71× trailing P/E any slowdown in revenue growth (currently running ~14%) or a miss on margin recovery post the one-off charges would compress the multiple sharply, and the high D/E of 9.6 flagged in the snapshot warrants close monitoring for interest coverage deterioration.

SBFC Finance is a mid-size NBFC focused on secured small-business loans (SME/MSME segment), with a loan book of ₹9,805 cr growing at 30.66% YoY — one of the stronger growth profiles among listed NBFCs. Revenue trajectory has been remarkably stable at ~28–31% YoY across all observable periods (FY26: +28.6%, Q3FY26: +27.7%, H1FY26: +30.7%), while PAT margins have gently expanded from 26.0% (Q1FY26) to 27.7% (Q3FY26), confirming operational leverage is working; the key credit-quality signal is encouraging — gross NPA has edged down from 2.78% (Q1FY26) to 2.61% (FY26), net NPA from 1.63% to 1.54%, and credit costs have normalised sharply from a distorted 5.59% (9M FY25 annualised) to 1.45% (FY26), while ROA has improved from 3.13% to 4.58%, all positive directional signals. Using the sector card's prescribed P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders: P/B of 2.71× against ROE of 13.0% sits in 'fair' territory — not cheap (P/B < 1.5 threshold) but not expensive either; peer-rank confirms this at P26–P34 across P/E and P/B, trading at a 36–41% discount to broad-market medians, though the correct peer set should be NBFC comps where 18–28× P/E is the norm, and at 22.4× trailing SBFC is at the lower end of that band, supporting a 'fair' grade; the forward P/E of 18.4× below trailing 22.4× signals the market is pricing in continued earnings growth, consistent with the AUM growth runway. The single biggest risk is the surge in impairment charges (+70.1% YoY to ₹125 cr) alongside negative CFO/PAT of -4.2× — loan book growth is consuming cash far faster than collections, and any credit-cycle deterioration or funding-cost spike (D/E at 192×) could rapidly compress ROA and compress the valuation multiple.

Emmvee Photovoltaic Power is a fast-growing Indian solar module manufacturer that doubled revenue to ₹5,049 cr in FY26 (+116% YoY) with PAT nearly tripling to ₹1,082 cr (+193% YoY), driven by a 9.4 GW order book (doubled from 4.9 GW), full transition to TOPCon technology, and strong operating leverage lifting EBITDA margins to ~34%; the company is a direct beneficiary of India's capex/PLI upcycle in renewables and the China+1 supply-chain shift. Sector KPIs are supportive — order book cover is substantial and order inflow was healthy at 4.5 GW in Q3FY26 alone, though Q4 inflow slowed to 1.27 GW, and execution growth at 116–118% appears to be plateauing at a high base rather than accelerating further. Valuation is genuinely cheap on earnings multiples — trailing P/E of 19.5× sits at the P20 percentile of the broad market and 40–45% below median, while EV/EBITDA of 13.4× is the more appropriate yardstick for this capital-intensive business and also screens at P21, well below the market median of 22.6×; however, the stock sits at 90% of its 52-week range, near highs, meaning the market has already partially re-rated it, and the forward P/E of 13.7× versus trailing 19.5× implies significant earnings growth is already consensus-priced in. The single biggest risk is the ₹4,500–4,800 cr module expansion capex plus ₹3,300 cr ingot-wafer facility commitment over FY27–FY30, which alongside a reported debt/equity of 9.74× (likely distorted by the recent IPO capital structure transition but still warrants scrutiny) and working capital buildup that compressed CFO to ₹200 cr versus PAT of ₹1,082 cr could stress the balance sheet if execution slips or solar module pricing softens.

Federal Bank is a Kerala-headquartered mid-sized private sector bank with a strong NRI deposit franchise (NRI deposits crossed ₹1 lakh cr, +13.2% YoY) and growing CASA franchise (CASA ratio 32.94%, up 271 bps YoY), competing in retail, commercial, and SME banking. Q4FY26 reported NII of ₹3,173 cr (+33% YoY) and underlying net profit of ₹1,145 cr (+10% YoY on an ex-one-off basis, though yfinance shows ₹1,341 cr including the ₹456 cr IT refund interest one-off and ₹115 cr tax reversal); revenue trajectory has accelerated meaningfully — Q3FY25 to Q4FY26 YoY NII growth stepped up from mid-teens to 33%, though underlying PAT growth is a more modest ~10% YoY once one-offs are stripped, with credit cost spiking to 118 bps in Q4FY26 vs 47 bps in Q4FY25 as a floating NPA provision was created. Trailing P/E of 17.1× sits within the 12–18× bank sector median (fair), P/B of 1.84× with ROE of 11.7% is marginally above the cheap threshold (P/B <1.5× with ROE >12%) but not expensive; peer rank at P46 confirms fairly valued vs sector, and a forward P/E of 12.6× below trailing suggests the market is pricing in continued earnings growth — however the stock sitting at 97% of its 52-week range limits near-term upside. The biggest risk is the credit cost trajectory: the jump to 118 bps in Q4FY26 (management guides 50–60 bps normalised) combined with West Asia geopolitical exposure via the NRI franchise and flat retail advances could pressure NIM and PAT growth if macro conditions deteriorate.

Piramal Finance (PIRAMALFIN) is a mid-size NBFC with a retail-heavy loan book of ₹84,927 cr (FY26), operating in housing finance, SME lending, and wholesale credit post-amalgamation with parent Piramal Enterprises in September 2025. FY26 revenue grew a strong +27.6% YoY to ₹13,157 cr and PAT surged +168% to ₹1,540 cr, but the headline PAT jump is substantially inflated by a ₹1,321.80 cr subsidiary dividend, a ₹263 cr Shriram Life stake-sale gain, and restated comparatives post-amalgamation — stripping one-offs, underlying earnings quality is questionable, and the 9M FY26 revenue trajectory of +13.7% shows meaningful deceleration from the full-year figure. Valuation yardstick per the sector card is P/B + ROE for lenders: at 1.6× P/B with ROE of only 5.4% (well below the 12% threshold for a 'cheap' read), PIRAMALFIN screens as fair-to-expensive on the correct metric, despite appearing cheap on forward P/E (13.8×, P21 in sector) — this apparent cheapness reflects depressed current ROE rather than genuine undervaluation, and the stock sitting at 88.9% of its 52-week range limits margin of safety. The single biggest risk is the combination of extreme leverage (net debt/EBITDA 33.2×, D/E 285.78×), deeply negative operating cash flow (CFO/PAT −10.26×, FCF −₹15,901 cr) driven by aggressive loan-book expansion, and rising credit costs (1.6% in Q3FY26) — any macro credit-cycle deterioration or wholesale funding-market stress could rapidly compress capital adequacy and ROE.

Cholamandalam Financial Holdings (CHOLAHLDNG) is a diversified Murugappa Group financial holding company with three key subsidiaries: CIFCL (NBFC, 43.76% stake), CMSGICL (general insurance, 60% stake), and a risk-services JV — CIFCL is the dominant earnings driver with AUM of ₹2.42L cr growing 21% YoY. Revenue growth has decelerated from +29.1% (Q3FY25) to +18.0% (FY26), but PAT margin has expanded from ~6.4% to 13.9% over the same window, driven by CIFCL PAT growing 23% YoY to ₹5,220 cr; the insurance subsidiary CMSGICL is a meaningful drag with PAT down 48% YoY to ₹253 cr due to equity fair-value adjustments. Using the Sector Card yardstick (P/B + ROE for NBFCs/lenders), P/B of 1.93× alongside TTM ROE of 18% screens cheap — P/B below 2× with ROE well above 12% is the 'cheap' zone — and the trailing P/E of 12.2× sits at the P10 percentile vs 499 broad-market peers (65.5% discount to median), though NBFC P/E benchmarks of 18–28× suggest the low multiple partly reflects holding-company structure and conglomerate discount rather than pure mispricing. The key risk is that EPS estimates have been revised down 6.1% over the past 30–90 days while CMSGICL continues to be a structural earnings drag through market-mark volatility, and at Debt/Equity of 621× (financial leverage normal for an NBFC but extreme by non-financial standards), any NIM compression or credit-cost deterioration at CIFCL would rapidly erode holding-company returns.

Groww (Billionbrains Garage Ventures) is India's largest retail stockbroking and financial-services platform by active users (~16.7 Mn as of Q4FY26), competing in the high-growth financialisation-of-savings theme against Zerodha, Angel One, and Upstox. Revenue growth has been volatile — +87.9% YoY in Q4FY26 (a small quarter at ₹147 cr) but the full-year FY26 picture shows +19% revenue and +14.2% PAT growth to ₹2,083 cr; importantly, PAT margin has been contracting, moving from 46.3% in Q2FY26 to 44.7% in Q4FY26, while cash conversion is deeply negative (CFO/PAT -0.01× in FY26 and -0.32× in Q2FY26), meaning reported profits are not yet translating into cash — a significant quality concern. On valuation, the stock trades at a trailing P/E of 59.2×, roughly 67% above the broad-market median of 35.4×, and at P/B of 12.85×; for a capital-markets / AMC-adjacent platform the most relevant yardstick per the sector card is P/EV or P/AUM-linked earnings rather than P/E, but on any conventional metric the stock sits at P90 in the broader peer set and is clearly expensive relative to the universe, partially offset by a forward P/E of 32× suggesting the market is pricing in strong earnings re-acceleration. The biggest fundamental risk is earnings quality: negative free cash flow, two loss-making subsidiaries (Fisdom and GroWWmf absorbing combined ₹316 Mn in Q4 losses), and a business model heavily correlated to market volumes and FII sentiment — any sustained equity-market downturn or regulatory tightening on discount broking could sharply compress both revenue and user engagement.

Elgi Equipments is a mid-cap manufacturer of air compressors and automotive equipment with a growing international footprint across 25 subsidiaries in the US, Europe, Brazil, Australia, and Asia — a niche industrial franchise with meaningful export exposure. Revenue growth has decelerated from +12.7% (9M FY26) to +9.9% (H1FY26) to +8.2% (Q1FY26) on a sequential quarterly read, though PAT growth has outpaced revenue at +21.8% YoY for 9M FY26 (₹30 cr) thanks to margin expansion — EBITDA margins improving to 17.4–18.5% range, with CFO/PAT of 1.28× confirming earnings are cash-backed; note the revenue figures in the trend table appear to be in USD millions or a sub-consolidated form and do not reconcile with the yfinance quarterly data (Q4FY26: ₹558 cr), suggesting the trend table covers a subsidiary/partial entity — I treat trajectory direction as reliable but absolute numbers with caution. At trailing P/E of 44.3× vs the Industrials sector median of 28–45×, the stock sits near the upper bound of fair — EV/EBITDA of 32× is 42% above the broad-market median (P67), and at 85.9% of its 52-week range the stock is priced for continued strong execution; forward P/E of 33× below trailing is a mild positive signal indicating consensus expects ~34% EPS growth, partially supported by estimate revisions of +2.8% over 90 days, but at these multiples any execution miss or capex-cycle slowdown would trigger a sharp de-rating. The single biggest risk is that the valuation yardstick here is EV/EBITDA for this capital-intensive exporter, and at 32× with D/E of 23.89 (high leverage flagged) and thin analyst coverage (4 analysts only), a global industrial slowdown or INR strengthening squeezing export competitiveness could compress both earnings and multiples simultaneously.

Indian Overseas Bank (IOB) is a mid-sized public sector bank (PSB) operating primarily in retail and MSME lending, with a significant turnaround story driven by aggressive NPA resolution over the past three years. The available data — anchored on H1FY26 — shows revenue growth of +12.6% YoY and a strong PAT trajectory with H1FY26 PAT of ₹2,437 cr representing +70.7% YoY growth (aided partly by the tax rate transition from 34.944% to 25.168% under Section 115BAA, and DTA benefits of ₹90,000 cr in 9M FY26), while the PCR stands at a best-in-class 97.49% and loan growth is robust at +21.65% YoY; however, the CAR has dipped from 17.94% in H1FY26 to 16.30% in Q3FY26, signalling capital consumption from loan-book expansion. Applying the Sector Card yardstick of P/B vs sustainable ROE: IOB trades at 1.83× P/B with TTM ROE of 15.7% — this screens as cheap (P/B < 1.5× with ROE > 12% = cheap per the desk rule; IOB is marginally above that P/B floor but still well below the 3× threshold for expensive), and the peer analysis confirms it sits at P10 on trailing P/E (13.1× vs broad market median 35.4×) and P14 on P/B, placing it unambiguously in the cheap quartile versus peers, although the forward P/E at 39.1× (P80 percentile) is a cautionary signal that the market anticipates earnings normalisation once one-off tax/DTA tailwinds fade. The single biggest fundamental risk is that the reported PAT improvement is substantially driven by non-recurring items — DTA reversals, tax-rate transition, and subsidiary wind-up proceeds — meaning sustainable normalised earnings power may be materially lower than headline figures suggest, and any re-rating toward fair value requires IOB to demonstrate clean, recurring earnings growth while managing the ₹3.6L cr+ contingent tax dispute overhang and continued capital adequacy under accelerating loan growth.

L&T Technology Services (LTTS) is a pure-play engineering R&D services company — one of India's largest ER&D players — operating across Mobility, Sustainability, and Tech segments after divesting the SWC business in FY26. FY26 full-year revenue grew 14% YoY in INR terms (₹109,959 Mn) on a continuing-operations basis, but USD revenue growth was only 8.3% and Q4 FY26 USD revenue growth decelerated sharply to just 0.3% YoY ($305.9 Mn), while PAT grew a modest 7.4% YoY to ₹12,818 Mn at an 11.7% margin — the gap between INR and USD growth is largely an INR depreciation tailwind that is now reversing given INR strengthening to 95.35. Trailing P/E of 28.2× sits at P71 vs IT sector peers and is +29% above the sector median of 21.8×; the forward P/E of 20.0× implies earnings growth is expected, but the EV/EBITDA of 18.3× is at P80 vs peers, making the stock expensive-to-fair relative to the peer set despite the 52-week low proximity (stock at only 15.1% of its 52-week range at ₹3,010–₹4,726). The biggest risk is the Mobility segment drag (−5% YoY) compounded by GenAI disruption to the ER&D services model, while the Q4 USD revenue near-stagnation signals that the FY26 large-deal TCV momentum ($855 Mn, +40% YoY) has not yet converted to sustained revenue acceleration — if macro headwinds persist into H1 FY27, consensus earnings estimates (reflected in the forward P/E) could prove too optimistic.

Union Bank of India is a mid-sized public sector bank (PSB) with ~₹1.3L cr market cap, operating across retail, MSME, and corporate lending segments with a growing emphasis on the RAM (Retail/Agriculture/MSME) book. The key trajectory signal is a sharp deceleration in revenue growth — from +10.1% in FY25 to near-flat (+0.1%) in FY26 — driven by NIM compression of 21 bps YoY (NIM falling from 2.91% to 2.70%) and a 1.49% decline in Net Interest Income; however, PAT margin has actually expanded sequentially from 12.9% in Q1FY26 to 16.2% in Q3FY26 and 17.6% for full FY26, largely due to dramatically lower credit costs (0.23% in FY26 vs 0.63% in Q3FY25) and strong NPA resolution (Gross NPA down 78 bps YoY to 2.82%, PCR at 95%). Using the sector card's prescribed P/B + ROE yardstick for lenders, UNIONBANK trades at P/B of 1.01× with ROE of 15.7%, which is unambiguously cheap — P/B below 1.5× with ROE well above 12% screens as cheap per the desk benchmark, and the peer rank at P3 (bottom 3rd percentile on P/E and P/B across 471 stocks) confirms deep valuation discount, though PSB discount is partly structural. The biggest risk is that NIM compression continues as EBLR-linked loans remain repriced down while deposit costs are slow to catch down, and the cost-to-income ratio has already deteriorated 350 bps YoY to 48.98%, leaving operating profit under pressure even as the credit cost tailwind fades.

Action Construction Equipment (ACE) is India's leading crane and construction-equipment manufacturer, commanding roughly 90% of its revenue from the cranes segment within a government-led capex and infrastructure upcycle. However, the multi-quarter revenue trajectory is clearly deteriorating: full-year FY26 revenue declined 1.4% YoY to ₹3,280 cr, with the trend worsening intra-year from -6.3% in H1FY26 to -11.2% in Q1FY26 (the most recent reported quarter), while the core cranes segment contracted 4.6% YoY — this deceleration from FY25's +14.2% growth is the primary concern. The partial offset is genuine: PAT margins have expanded steadily (12.3% FY25 → 12.7% FY26, with Q1FY26 at 13.9%), PAT grew 1.4% YoY to ₹415 cr despite the revenue headwind, and FY26 CFO/PAT of 1.01x confirms earnings are cash-backed; on valuation, trailing P/E of 28x sits within the Industrials sector median range of 28–45x (fair on P/E), EV/EBITDA of 20.7x is below the broad-market peer median of 22.6x (P45), and forward P/E of 21.5x below trailing signals the market is pricing in earnings recovery — overall a fair valuation, not a clear mispricing. The biggest risk is that the revenue contraction in the core cranes segment deepens if government capex execution slows or private-sector equipment demand remains soft, which would erode the margin-expansion story and compress the re-rating thesis given thin sell-side coverage and recent slight downward EPS revisions.

Mphasis is a mid-tier Indian IT services company with a strong focus on Banking & Financial Services (BFS) and direct business, competing against peers like Coforge and Persistent in niche digital transformation. FY26 full-year revenue grew 6.7% YoY in constant currency, with Q4FY26 accelerating to +7.1% YoY (₹3,107 cr) and EPS rising to ₹26.70 vs ₹23.13 in Q3FY25 — a modestly positive trajectory, though the ITO service line contracted 21.6% YoY due to deliberate ATM business scale-down, and the Logistics & Transportation vertical collapsed 54.3% YoY, partially masking the underlying BFS/Insurance strength (+17% and +46% YoY respectively). At a trailing P/E of 24.7× against the sector median of 22–30×, Mphasis sits at P67 among IT peers — a mild premium to median (19×) but well below high-growth peers Coforge and Persistent; forward P/E of 18.3× implies earnings growth is expected, and EV/EBITDA at 14.7× is at the sector peer median, making the stock broadly fairly valued. The biggest risk is that record TCV of $2.1Bn (+68% YoY) and a 69% AI-led pipeline fail to convert to revenue at the pace implied by FY27 guidance of high single-digit to low double-digit growth, especially if macro uncertainty delays BFS client decision cycles or the structural AI disruption headwind compresses deal pricing faster than management currently anticipates.

HDB Financial Services (HDBFS) is a large NBFC (HDFC Bank subsidiary) focused on retail and SME lending, recently listed on NSE in July 2025 under RBI's NBFC Upper Layer framework; it occupies a mid-tier position in the organised NBFC space with a loan book of roughly ₹1.1L cr. Revenue growth has been solid at +13–21% YoY across recent quarters and PAT grew +16.9% in FY26 to ₹2,544 cr, but loan growth is decelerating (14.3% → 12.2% → 11.0% YoY) and credit costs remain elevated at 2.58% of the loan book — well above management's own 2.3% medium-term target — with Gross NPA at 2.44% and Net NPA at 1.09%, both still under pressure through Q3FY26 before showing only marginal Q4 improvement. Valuation on the correct NBFC yardstick (P/B + ROE): P/B of 2.79× against ROE of 13.9% is roughly fair — the sector card's benchmark suggests P/B < 1.5× + ROE > 12% = cheap, P/B > 3× + ROE < 12% = expensive; HDBFS sits in the middle with adequate but not outstanding ROE, and at P27 in the broad-market peer set (trailing P/E -36% vs median) it looks superficially cheap on earnings multiples, but the more relevant P/B-to-ROE relationship argues 'fair' rather than cheap, especially with sustained downward EPS revisions (-1.5% over 90 days). The single biggest risk is that credit costs fail to moderate toward the guided 2.3% range — the current 2.58% run-rate, combined with negative operating cash flow (CFO/PAT of -0.34× in FY26), means any further asset-quality deterioration in the unsecured or microfinance segments would compress ROE and pressure the P/B multiple simultaneously.

New India Assurance (NIACL) is India's largest public-sector general insurer by gross premium, but its core underwriting business is structurally loss-making — the combined ratio stands at 108.4% in Q3FY26 (and a deeply distressed 139.5% in H1FY26), meaning every rupee of premium written generates a net underwriting loss, with Fire (₹-550 cr) and Motor (₹-4,563 cr) segments both technically underwater in FY26; profitability is almost entirely dependent on investment income (yield 8.92%), which masks the operating deterioration. Revenue growth has been moderate and volatile (+5.7% FY25, +9.7% Q2FY26, +13.2% FY26 — directionally acceptable), but PAT margins oscillate wildly (0.2% in Q2FY26, 12.6% in Q3FY26, 41.6% in Q1FY26 vs 2.7% FY25 full year) reflecting lumpiness in claims and exceptional items rather than structural improvement, and cash flow conversion is deeply negative (CFO/PAT -0.25x FY26, -9.95x H1FY26) — a serious quality flag. Valuation appears statistically cheap: P/B of 0.76× and forward P/E of 9.2× place it at P1–P7 vs 471 peers, but the Sector Card instructs us to use P/B + ROE for insurers — with ROE at just 3.4% (far below the 12% threshold for P/B cheapness to be meaningful), the low P/B is a value trap signal, not a bargain, and the correct yardstick here is combined ratio and underwriting profitability trends, both of which are deteriorating. The biggest risk is the qualified audit opinion (unresolved reinsurance and inter-office reconciliation), a ₹91,200 cr cumulative GST dispute (stays currently in place at Bombay HC), wage revision arrears of ₹249 cr, and FY-EPS estimates cut 22–26% over the past 90 days — this constellation of governance, regulatory, and earnings-revision risks overwhelms the statistical cheapness.

AU Small Finance Bank is a high-growth small finance bank transitioning to a universal bank, with a strong retail-secured and commercial banking franchise that grew its gross loan portfolio 21% YoY to ₹1,40,327 cr in FY26, significantly outpacing estimated private sector credit growth of ~13%. Revenue grew 14.7% YoY to ₹12,091 cr in FY26 while PAT grew 25% YoY to ₹2,641 cr (margin ~21.9%), with Q4FY26 PAT surging 65% YoY to ₹832 cr — though this reflects seasonal strength and some credit-cost tailwind (60bps in Q4 vs guided 90bps for FY27), so the trajectory is accelerating at the headline level but with a cautionary note that full-year ROA of 1.6% lagged Q4's 1.8%. Trailing P/E of 27.8× sits 42% above the sector median of 19.6× and P/B of 3.6× is at the 75th percentile among peers — for a bank with ROE implicitly ~14-15% (PAT ₹2,641 cr on ~₹18,000 cr book), this P/B premium is partly justified by growth but leaves the stock fairly valued to mildly expensive relative to peers, especially since forward P/E of 16× implies significant earnings growth that hinges on credit cost discipline. The key risk is that credit costs for FY27 are guided higher at ~90bps versus Q4FY26's 60bps, and the digital unsecured / credit card book (down 10% YoY) has been a multi-quarter drag — any re-acceleration of stress in the unsecured segment or NIM compression from higher funding costs could pressure the 1.8% ROA target management is banking on.

Tata Chemicals is a global soda ash and specialty chemicals producer (India, US, UK, Kenya) with a growing non-soda ash portfolio (bicarb, silica, salt, Rallis agri-inputs) that now contributes ~48% of FY26 consolidated revenue of ₹14,584 cr. Revenue declined 2% YoY in FY26 and EBITDA fell 8% to ₹1,805 cr (12.4% margin, down 60bps), while reported PAT collapsed 49.7% to ₹241 cr on a pre-exceptional basis — and turned deeply negative at the consolidated level due to a ₹1,837 cr US goodwill impairment and ₹182 cr deferred tax write-off; Q4FY26 standalone PAT was -₹279 cr before exceptionals versus -₹12 cr a year earlier, a sharp sequential and YoY deterioration driven by soda ash pricing at multi-year lows and elevated global inventories. EV/EBITDA of 14.5× sits modestly below the sector peer median of 16.5× (P43 rank) and well below the specialty/materials premium peers, while P/B of 0.82× is at P0 (cheapest in sector), but these apparently cheap multiples are mechanically suppressed by deeply negative trailing ROE (-7.7%) and a leveraged balance sheet (net debt ₹5,961 cr, D/E 36×), making them unreliable value signals rather than genuine cheapness. The single biggest risk is a prolonged soda ash down-cycle: Chinese domestic prices are down ~54% from Q3FY23 peaks, global inventories remain elevated at ~1.8 MT, and management has explicitly guided for flat near-term demand — any further price erosion or delay in the cycle recovery would extend losses in the US and UK segments, threaten interest coverage on the high debt load, and could trigger additional impairments.

RBL Bank is a mid-size private sector lender (~₹22,872 cr market cap) that has been executing a turnaround after a period of elevated stress, with its key differentiator being rapid asset-quality improvement and strong loan growth; the Emirates NBD strategic investment (pending final closure) adds a credible anchor-investor narrative. Latest full-year FY26 numbers show revenue growth of just +2% YoY (essentially flat, with NII actually declining 2% YoY) while PAT grew 18% YoY to ₹822 cr — driven more by sharply lower credit costs (GNPA fell from 2.78% in Q1FY26 to 1.45% by FY26-end, a dramatic sequential improvement) than by top-line momentum; this PAT recovery is real but fragile given the NIM compression of 61 bps to 4.51% and a cost-to-income ratio that worsened to 68.52%. Using the sector-card yardstick of P/B vs sustainable ROE for lenders: P/B at 1.36× is cheap in absolute terms (sector card norm for P/B+ROE; ROA 0.53% implies ROE roughly 8–9%, which is sub-par), and the stock sits at only P9 among ~471 peers on P/B, making it optically cheap — however, with ROE well below the 12% threshold where P/B < 1.5 would be unambiguously attractive, the low P/B reflects justified skepticism rather than hidden value. The single biggest risk is that NIM compression persists — NII declined even as loans grew 23% YoY, meaning the bank is growing volume but losing spread, and with CAR declining QoQ to 14.25% and CET-1 at 12.77% (still above regulatory minimum but thinning), capital adequacy could constrain further growth or require dilutive equity raising before the Emirates NBD deal closes.

Balkrishna Industries is a global niche leader in Off-Highway Tyres (OHT), with a presence in 160+ countries and a dominant position in agricultural and construction tyres; it is now extending into On-Highway (CV Radial, PCR) and Carbon Black segments targeting 2.2× revenue growth to ₹23,000 cr by FY30. FY26 (consolidated) delivered revenue growth of just +3.6% YoY to ₹10,823 cr while PAT declined sharply by -24.9% YoY to ₹1,243 cr — a multi-quarter trajectory of margin compression (EBITDA margin down ~252 bps to 22.4–22.7%, PAT margin down ~380 bps to 11.2–11.5%) driven by higher finance costs on a rising debt load (net debt ₹4,045 cr vs near net-cash in 9MFY25), exceptional items, and US tariff headwinds that cut Americas volumes ~30% YoY. At trailing P/E of 33.6× and EV/EBITDA of 19.5× the stock sits at the sector median on P/E but at P75 on EV/EBITDA (40% premium to sector median of 13.9×), placing it in 'fair-to-expensive' territory relative to Auto peers, though the forward P/E of 21.9× (significant discount to trailing) signals meaningful earnings recovery is already priced in by the market — the stock is near its 52-week low at 18% of range, reflecting current fundamental weakness rather than pure value. The single biggest risk is capex execution: ₹6,800 cr committed through FY29 has already flipped FCF negative (₹-754 cr FY26) and pushed net debt/EBITDA to 1.67×, and any demand shortfall — particularly in the US given ongoing tariff uncertainty — could further stress coverage ratios and delay the FY30 margin recovery thesis.

360 ONE WAM is India's leading integrated private wealth and asset management platform, managing ₹6.74 lakh crore in total AUM, with a capital-light ARR (recurring fee) revenue stream of ₹2,289 Cr (+34.5% YoY) and ARR retention improving to 78 bps from 73 bps — a meaningful stickiness signal. FY26 revenue grew 29.4% YoY (consistent with FY25's 32.5%), PAT grew 20.7% to ₹1,225 Cr, but PAT margin contracted sharply to 28.1% from 38.3% in FY25; this compression is partly structural — Other Income collapsed 63% (₹313 Cr → ₹116 Cr), inflating FY25's base — but expenses also grew 28.7% YoY, nearly matching revenue growth, limiting operating leverage. Using EV/EBITDA of 21.4× (the right yardstick per the sector card for a capital-markets-linked business) the stock sits at P47 vs broad-market peers, a slight discount to the 22.6× median, and forward P/E of 27.4× is meaningfully below trailing 39.2×, implying the market prices in strong earnings recovery — grading as fair, not cheap. The single biggest risk is the March 2025 Income Tax Department search with a ₹336 Cr contingent liability (outcome uncertain), compounded by 90-day sell-side EPS estimate cuts of ~3.5% — a pattern that can precede derating even when headline growth remains healthy.
